strengths: The paper addresses a useful computer-vision problem: generating image-specific categories for segmentation without requiring users to supply a vocabulary. The framework requires no additional model training and builds on clearly identified pretrained components.

BBoost offers a technically interesting approach to local captioning through multiresolution BLIP feature clustering, cluster alignment, denoising, and decoding selected patch embeddings. This provides a concrete mechanism for discovering categories missed by global captions.

Experiments span four datasets and include relevant alternatives using the same segmentor. Table 3 reports substantial VOC improvements over LLaVA + X-Decoder (87.1 versus 56.7 mIoU), while Table 1 supports the benefit over plain BLIP captioning across all four datasets.

LAVE addresses a genuine difficulty in evaluating generated category names. Its results are within 1.1 mIoU of manual mappings on all four datasets, providing useful supporting evidence. The supplementary prompts, pseudocode, intermediate visualizations, and candid failure examples improve transparency.
weaknesses: LAVE has unresolved validity issues. Section 9.3 instructs the evaluator to map 'stuff' categories to background even for datasets that annotate such categories. For Context and ADE20K, it also relies on the LLM recalling the dataset vocabulary instead of supplying the actual list. Algorithm 1 preserves exact label matches, but synonymous stuff labels remain vulnerable. Aggregate agreement with manual mappings is reassuring, yet a classwise audit is needed to establish correctness.

The model-selection protocol is insufficiently specified. Section 5.1 describes evaluation on validation datasets and Bayesian hyperparameter optimization on VOC without identifying a separate tuning split. Tables 2–4 use the best caption-cycle count for each dataset. Without held-out selection and repeated stochastic runs, the reported performance may be optimistic, particularly for the small Context improvement over ZeroSeg.

Comparison with the closest prior work is not demonstrably controlled. The manuscript does not establish whether ZeroSeg was reevaluated using the same mapper and background/ignore conventions. This matters because Table A7 changes VOC performance by 9.6–13.2 points solely through the mapping method. The captioning baselines also lack sufficient decoding-budget and configuration details to isolate the benefit of BBoost.

The central claim of richer open-ended recognition is supported mainly by selected visual examples and generated-vocabulary counts. More generated names do not establish more correct discoveries, and mapping predictions back to fixed labels cannot verify fine-grained naming accuracy. A representative assessment of novel-category precision, coverage, and hallucinations would strengthen this contribution substantially.

The novelty should be framed more narrowly: ZeroSeg already addresses segmentation without a supplied vocabulary, so introducing AVS as a new task is overstated. The distinctive contribution is the BLIP-based regional captioning pipeline and evaluator. Although integration with arbitrary OVS models is plausible, experiments demonstrate BBoost with only X-Decoder.

Several reproducibility details need clarification: Equation 9 describes independent maximum-IoU assignments rather than the stated Hungarian matching; alignment between the two spatial grids and handling appended positional dimensions before frozen BLIP decoding are underspecified. Table A6 states one captioning cycle but reports 87.1 mIoU, whereas Table 2 reports 85.3 for one cycle. Runtime and memory measurements are also absent despite efficiency and scalability claims.
